name: Cube
summary: An open-source, headless semantic layer: define metrics, joins and access rules once in YAML, query them over SQL, REST or GraphQL, and serve repeated queries from rollups it builds ahead of time.
intro: Cube sits between a SQL data source and everything that reads from it. You describe the data in cubes (entities such as orders, with their measures, dimensions and joins) and views (curated datasets built from cubes), in YAML or JavaScript files kept in git. Consumers query those names through a Postgres-compatible SQL API, REST (JSON) or GraphQL, and AI agents through an MCP server. Cube checks each query against the model, applies access policies, generates SQL in the source’s dialect and returns the result. It connects to warehouses such as Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and ClickHouse, query engines such as Athena, Trino and DuckDB, and application databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL. It has no UI of its own: that is what “headless” means here.

Its cache is where it becomes a static read model. Pre-aggregations are rollup tables declared in the data model, for example revenue and order count by status and month. A refresh worker builds them in the background and stores them in Cube Store, a distributed engine written in Rust on Apache Arrow and DataFusion that keeps the data as Parquet files in S3, Google Cloud Storage or MinIO. When a query arrives, Cube’s aggregate awareness finds a matching rollup and answers from it instead of the warehouse. Each rollup has a refresh key, every hour by default, or a cheap SQL check such as `SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM orders` that triggers a rebuild only when the data changed. Cube Core is the open-source project; Cube, the company’s commercial product, adds workbooks, dashboards, an analytics chat, hosting and more on the same model.
strengths: One model for every consumer: SQL, REST, GraphQL and MCP interfaces mean BI tools, apps and AI agents get the same metric definitions and access rules
Pre-aggregations answer matching queries from Cube Store without touching the warehouse, and a rollup-only mode lets the warehouse stay suspended between refreshes
Incremental, partitioned rollups refresh only recent partitions (say the last three months), which cuts rebuild time and cost on per-scan warehouses such as BigQuery and Athena
Code-first and open: Apache 2.0 backend, models in git, and a data model that runs unchanged in Cube Core and the commercial Cube
limits: Development mode is an authentication bypass: with `CUBEJS_DEV_MODE=true` the REST and GraphQL APIs accept requests without a token, so it must never be reachable from the internet
Rollups only help queries they match; anything else goes to the source, or fails in rollup-only mode on a single node, so the set of pre-aggregations needs ongoing tuning
Rollups are only as fresh as their refresh key, and builds queue when there are too many partitions: Cube’s guidance is to avoid more than 64, and fewer when a rollup has extra indexes
It needs a SQL source: Cube isn’t built to read files or REST APIs directly (use DuckDB for Parquet on S3), and some drivers need write access to build rollups in the source first
Several conveniences, such as importing dbt models and scheduled dashboard refreshes, are Premium features of the commercial Cube rather than part of Cube Core

sections.title: Cube’s two cache levels
sections.intro: Both are on the read path; only the second is computed ahead of time.

rows.label: What it stores
values: Results of queries already run, keyed by the generated SQL
Rollup tables declared in the data model, stored as Parquet in Cube Store

rows.label: When it’s filled
values: On the first request for a query
Ahead of time, by a background refresh worker

rows.label: When it’s refreshed
values: When the cube’s refresh key changes; checked every 2 minutes on Athena, BigQuery, Databricks, Firebolt, Presto and Snowflake, every 10 seconds elsewhere
Every hour by default, or when a refresh SQL check returns a new value; partitioned rollups can refresh only a recent window

story: Artyom Keydunov and Pavel Tiunov founded Statsbot in 2016, a business intelligence tool that pulled reports into Slack. To power it they built an engine that generated SQL, cached results and handled security between databases and the front end. Statsbot’s users kept asking whether they could use that engine for their own internal or customer-facing analytics, so the founders released it on its own as Cube.js, an open-source analytics framework, in 2019, launching it on Hacker News.

Cube.js already sped up queries with pre-aggregations, but they lived in the source database or a separate PostgreSQL or MySQL instance, and that store became the bottleneck for concurrency and latency. In April 2021 Cube Store became generally available: a pre-aggregation store written entirely in Rust on Arrow, DataFusion and Parquet. By August 2022 more of the code was Rust than JavaScript, distribution had moved from npm to Docker, and the company dropped the “.js”: Cube.js became Cube, a headless BI platform.

The company now sells Cube as an agentic analytics platform with workbooks, dashboards and an AI chat built on the same model, and maintains the open-source part as Cube Core. Its pitch for a semantic layer has shifted with it: agents that write SQL against raw tables produce inconsistent metrics, while agents that query a governed model get consistent ones.

choices.choice: Headless: APIs instead of a UI
choices.why: Statsbot’s users wanted the engine behind their own apps and dashboards, so Cube exposes SQL, REST and GraphQL and leaves the visualisation to whatever sits on top.

Keeping pre-aggregations in PostgreSQL or MySQL limited concurrency and latency and lacked features such as approximate distinct counts, so Cube built Cube Store as a drop-in replacement that scales out with more workers.
The team wanted low-level performance for the store and built on existing open-source pieces: Parquet for data at rest, Arrow in memory and DataFusion to execute queries.
Data models, configuration and access policies are files in version control, so changes go through review and CI, and AI tools can propose edits through the same workflow.
